name: Duna
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Lexical roots in Duna are realised with contrastive pitch contours, and the language exhibits a word tone system in that "the word as a whole is more important than the syllable as a domain for the assignment of tones" (Donohue 1997:360). Contrastive tone melodies are contracted or stretched to fit as many syllables as there are in the word. [...] My understanding of Duna tone is preliminary and I have not achieved a coherent analysis of Duna tone as a linguistic system [...] (p. 55) I describe monomorphemic lexical roots in Duna as being realised with one of four pitch contours: fall (F), rise (R), convex (C), or level (LV). (p. 56)
new_statements.citation: San Roque, Lila. 2008. An introduction to Duna grammar. PhD thesis, Australian National University.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Duna is described as a word-tone language: every monomorphemic (non-verb) root carries one lexically specified pitch contour (fall, rise, convex or level; probably three underlying melodies H, LH, HL) that stretches over the whole word whatever its syllable count. The grammar contains no statement about word stress at all, neither a stress rule nor an explicit denial of stress; the only word-level prosodic contrast described is tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Rise vs convex not contrastive on monosyllables; fall vs convex not contrastive on polysyllables (p. 67), so contrast is at most three-way. Verbs and polymorphemic words are not analysed; some consonantal/wa-class verb pairs are distinguished by pitch only (sa- 'take' level vs sa- 'strike' rising, p. 82). Giles (MS) quoted in fn. on p. 55: 'Duna is a tone language... syllables may have a mid, high, level, rising, or falling tone'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (word tone) on monomorphemic non-verb roots of up to three syllables, elicited in citation form / isolation; F0 traces from Praat. Data are Lake Kopiago (north-western) Duna.
new_statements.identity_note: San Roque 2008 describes Duna as spoken in the Lake Kopiago area (north-western dialect); the older Giles materials describe the south-eastern (Kelabo/Koroba) variety, which San Roque says differs only slightly. duna1248 is the language-level code; Glottolog gives no separate dialect codes. Note that six of the eleven Glottolog 'descriptive' references for duna1248 (Edwards 2002, Darcy et al. 2009, Elman & McClelland 1988, Kong et al. 2017, Edwards 2014, Bastiaanse 2011) are aphasia/psycholinguistics papers mis-assigned to Duna and are not about this language.

sources.note: Chapter 2 (Phonology) never mentions stress or accent; the only suprasegmental treated is contrastive word-level pitch: §2.2 'Contrastive lexical pitch on monomorphemic words' (pp. 55-68) describes Duna as a word-tone language with four citation pitch contours (fall, rise, convex, level), possibly three underlying melodies (H, LH, HL), on non-verb roots of up to three syllables in citation form; the author calls her tone analysis preliminary. A full-text grep for 'stress'/'accent' finds only non-phonological uses.
Tertiary; paraphrases San Roque 2008 on the four pitch contours; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Gillespie, Kirsty & Lila San Roque. 2011. Music and language in Duna pikono. In A. Rumsey & D. Niles (eds.), Sung tales from the Papua New Guinea Highlands, 49-63. Canberra: ANU E Press.
sources.note: Analyses melodic contour and line structure of sung tales; no statement on word stress or on the lexical tone system (the 'accented syllables' remark on p. 67 of the volume belongs to a different chapter).

sources.note: Ethnomusicography; p. 28 states second-hand 'Duna is recognised as a tonal language, using a "word-tone" system (Donohue 1997) with three or possibly four alternative tonal contours that extend across the length of a single word, regardless of how many syllables it has... (San Roque 2004)'. No mention of stress.
